title: Erie Canal Lock 23 to Lock 8
summary: Mid 70s, overcast, light winds, with canal sections at flood stage after five days of heavy rain.
body:
We departed Erie Canal Lock 23 at 0648 on September 23, 2021 aboard a Hatteras 75 Panacera, expecting this to be part of the home stretch into Troy and the final eastbound push on the Erie Canal.

But the canal had other ideas.

The previous five days had brought so much rain to the region that several sections were at flood stage. Around the locks, the dams were pushing huge amounts of water, and many of the downstream exits were far more turbulent than normal. Conditions for the day itself were not especially dramatic, mid-70s, overcast, light winds, but the canal system was clearly still carrying a lot more water than usual.

Even so, most of the day went smoothly.

The problem came just after Lock 8.

We approached a bridge we had passed under without issue on the westbound trip earlier that spring. As usual, the mate was in position on the ladder checking overhead clearance. Instead of the expected all-clear, he called down that we did not have room, and not by a little. We were somewhere around six to eight inches too tall for the bridge in the canal’s current state.

With current running and no interest in learning that lesson the expensive way, I brought the boat as close as I was comfortable to confirm it was real and not an optical illusion.

It was real.

We called the canal authority and reported the estimated clearance issue. They created an alert, and we turned around, locked back through Lock 8, and tied up on the calm side above the lock wall. After that, there was not much to do except let the system catch up.

So we secured the boat, talked with the lock master for a while, and then rode our electric scooters to the nearest restaurant for a decent lunch. Later we rode down the bike path to the bridge itself and took a few pictures of the water level. The lock master guessed they would have the canal dropped enough by around 0900 or 1000 the next morning.

At 0800 the next day we rode back to check it again and could already see how much difference the canal authority had made. It was actually impressive to watch that system do exactly what it was designed to do. We waited another hour just to be safe, then got underway again.

This time we had a little over two inches to spare.

We only made 74 nautical miles that day, and the canal bought itself one more day with us than we had planned on giving it. But it also reinforced a lesson that is easy to get lazy about in familiar water: procedure matters every time. It did not matter that we had already passed under that bridge months earlier. The mate checked clearance like he was supposed to, and that saved us from a very embarrassing and very expensive mistake.

title: Flying Fish Marina to Staniel Cay
summary: A long calm run from Long Island back toward Staniel Cay got Lady B back on schedule, with whales on departure and an improvised trolling session at the cut while waiting for the slip to open.
body:
We departed Flying Fish Marina in Clarence Town, Long Island, on March 20, 2023 aboard *Lady B*, an 85-foot Pacific Mariner, bound for Staniel Cay.

This was the last long passage with the owner and guests still aboard at the tail end of a months-long Bahamas trip. Weather had already delayed our departure by a couple of days, which killed the original plan of working our way back north by shorter island-hopping legs. The guests had departure flights out of Nassau coming up, so we needed to cover a big section of the southern Exumas in one shot and get them back into the neighborhood for the final few days of the trip.

It turned into exactly the kind of day you hope for when the schedule has started to tighten.

Conditions on departure were 76.8°F with light SSE winds around 9 knots. By arrival they had shifted slightly to about 10 knots from the SSW, temperature 74.7°F, with calm seas all day. The gentle wind stayed at our back, the boat ran well, and the guests were actually able to enjoy the day instead of spending it stressed about timing or beat up by weather.

We saw whales on departure, then settled into a smooth run up the sound. By the end of the day we had covered 113 nautical miles in just under nine hours.

The only wrinkle came at Staniel. When we got to the cut, I called Patrice on the radio and found out our slip at the marina was not cleared out yet. She asked if we could give it another hour before coming in.

So we turned around and improvised.

The guests rigged some lines and we went trolling with an 85-foot motoryacht, which is not the most dignified look but got the job done. We ended up landing a four-foot barracuda, which was also the day I learned that our deckhand’s fishing skills were mostly fictional. Fortunately the chef was a real fisherman and stepped in, handled the whole thing cleanly, got the trophy photos, and saw to it that the fish was safely released.

That killed just enough time for our slip to open up. We got into the marina, got everything unstowed, and had the boat settled in time for dinner.

What I remember most about that day is how pleasant it was in spite of the schedule pressure hanging behind it. No weather, no drama, no guest anxiety, just a smooth run, a little improvisation at the end, and the feeling that we had gotten back on schedule without anybody having to suffer for it. After a long trip, that kind of day stands out.

title: New York Harbor Arrival on Lady Victory
summary: Took command less than a day before departure from Florida, learned the boat underway, then entered New York Harbor on the first nice June weekend with the radar finally back online and a screen full of traffic.
body: I took command of the boat less than 24 hours before departure from Florida and had to learn it all the way up the coast. A few low sleep days into my command we were passing under the Verrazzano Bridge into lower New York Harbor. I had finally repaired the radar and plotter, and it was the first nice June weekend day in New York, so when I entered the harbor the spiderweb of target tracks that appeared on the screen made for a distinct change in operation from the offshore Atlantic run of the previous few days.

title: Crossing to Chub Cay
summary: Seed example log entry for a South Florida to Bahamas crossing day, structured to power both homepage recents and Travel Trail archive views.
body:
This is a seed example log entry, meant to prove the content model rather than claim a final polished narrative.

Left South Florida on a clean enough weather window and settled into the crossing rhythm, the kind where the job becomes less about talking and more about paying attention. The point of a log like this in the system is not just to hold prose, but to pin a dated movement to real places, a real chapter arc, and supporting images that can back up the memory later.

As the run moved east, the crossing stopped being an abstract line on a map and became the emotional hinge between familiar water and island water. That is exactly the kind of transition the archive should be able to show, not only in photos, but in written material that can appear on the homepage as a recent log and still live permanently inside the full Travel Trail archive.

Arrival at Chub Cay gives the entry a clear destination anchor, but the important structural point is that this one log can relate to Fort Lauderdale, the crossing itself, Chub Cay, the Exploration Years chapter, and multiple images without duplicating anything.

title: Boca to Boca, With a Steering Problem in the Middle
summary: Around 80°F with light SSE wind, good conditions for an easy owner day cruise.
body:
We departed The Boca Raton on March 24, 2025 aboard *Lady Victory* for what was supposed to be a simple owner cruise, a pleasant run out of the home slip, down toward Fort Lauderdale, and back. The plan was easy enough: ICW to Hillsboro Inlet, out to the ocean, back in through Port Everglades, then a relaxed ride north on the ICW to Boca. Conditions were good, around 80 degrees with light SSE wind, and nothing about the day suggested it was going to become particularly educational.

For the most part, it did not.

The owners had friends aboard and were just out for a boat ride. While we were offshore between Pompano and Fort Lauderdale, I handed the wheel to the mate so I could do a quick engine room check and step away for a minute. When I came back up, he showed me that the rudder indicator was no longer responding to wheel input. The boat was still tracking straight and we were only making about five to six knots, but it was immediately clear that something in the steering system was no longer behaving normally.

I went back down to the engine room and found the reservoir for the power steering pump empty.

I topped it off, repressurized the system, and confirmed over the radio with the mate that steering response had returned. That got us moving normally again, and we continued into Port Everglades. While we were waiting on the Las Olas bridge, I went back down and found the reservoir about halfway drained again. So from there on out, the trip became a quiet exercise in keeping the system alive long enough to get home cleanly. I kept adding fluid, kept checking levels, and kept us moving.

From the guest side, it was still just a nice day on the boat.

That was the whole point.

We completed the trip and made it back to the slip without the owners or their guests ever really knowing there had been an issue. The main challenge, other than the actual steering problem, was trying to keep my uniform looking vaguely presentable while repeatedly disappearing to deal with power steering fluid.

Once we were back, I told the boss what had happened and went straight into the lazarette to find the missing fluid. It was not hard to locate. Most of it was in the bilge, and the source turned out to be a steering hose that had very nearly ruptured completely. That afternoon I had new steering lines made, and the mate and I replaced them.

What stays with me about that day is that from the outside it looked like nothing had happened. Sometimes that is what a successful day actually looks like. Not heroics, not drama, just finding the problem, managing it calmly, and getting everybody home before the issue gets a chance to introduce itself properly.

title: New York to Portsmouth Instead of Virginia Beach
summary: Departure cold but calm; arrival cold and blowing, with seas building near the mouth of the Chesapeake.
body:
We departed Chelsea Piers in New York on the evening of October 7, 2025 aboard *Lady Victory*, starting south on the seasonal delivery run out of the city. The original destination was the Virginia Beach Fishing Center.

By the time we left, we were already a few days behind schedule. The boat had mechanically protested getting underway in the first place, and the weather window was starting to narrow. Departure from New York Harbor was cold but calm, and for most of the overnight run the trip was fairly uneventful.

As morning came on, the weather started to shift.

We were in contact with Virginia Beach Fishing Center as we approached. That inlet can be unpredictable even on a good day, and they were already reporting shoaling. Local traffic moving through was still giving usable guidance on where the safe water was, and based on those reports we were not especially worried about our 5.5-foot draft. At that stage, getting in still looked possible.

But the closer we got, the less attractive that plan became.

Near the mouth of the Chesapeake, with Virginia Beach only another hour to hour and a half away, the seas were continuing to build and the forecast for the next few days was looking worse, not better. Even if we got in, there was a good chance we would be stuck there for several days. And once the weather passed, there was no telling what the shoaling at the inlet would look like afterward. We were close enough to make it work, but no longer close enough to justify it.

So we changed the plan and diverted to Tidewater Yacht Marina in Portsmouth instead.

It was the safer option, the more stable option, and it also set us up well for the next day. With weather shutting down the outside route anyway, Portsmouth positioned us to continue south on the ICW instead of gambling on a sketchy arrival and then sitting around trapped behind worsening conditions.

We did not get tied up until around midnight, so it made for a long day. But it was still the right call. Better to end tired in the right place than spend the night congratulating yourself for forcing the original plan.

That run stands out because there was no dramatic emergency, just the steady narrowing of a bad option until the smarter one became obvious. Those are the decisions that keep trips moving.

title: Leaving Lake Worth with the Sunrise
summary: Grey and overcast with following seas making for a smooth northbound outside ride.
body:
I left Palm Harbor Marina this morning on a northbound delivery and made the 6:45 bridge opening to get out Lake Worth Inlet right at sunrise.

That part of the day had a good look to it, even if it was not exactly a dramatic Florida postcard morning. Everything was a little grey and overcast, but the light coming up over the inlet still gave the run a proper start. Once outside, I turned north and settled in on the ocean with St. Augustine as the goal for the day.

It has been an easy ride so far. The sky has stayed dull, but the following seas have kept things smooth, which is a trade I will take every time. There is not much to complain about when the boat is moving well, the inlet is behind you, and the day opens up in front of you one clean leg at a time.

For now this is the start of another northbound string, with today aimed at St. Augustine and the rest of the trip to follow from there.

By the time I was passing Cape Canaveral, the day had improved properly. The sea state had laid right down into flat calm, the sky had gone full blue, and the boat was moving at 18.5 knots with 84 nautical miles left to St. Augustine. Those are the sort of conditions that make it hard to complain about anything. I would happily run in weather like that all the time.

The day finished cleanly. We made St. Augustine at 6:38 and came to the Bridge of Lions right on 7:00 for the 7 p.m. opening. We were docked at St. Augustine Municipal Marina by 7:15, which made it 12 and a quarter hours dock to dock. By 8:00 the boat was rinsed down and fueled up, and that was good enough for the day. Now it is dinner, sleep, and a 6 a.m. departure tomorrow heading for Charleston.

title: Leaving St. Augustine at Sunrise
summary: Beautiful sunrise departure with a light 1-2 foot swell on the starboard quarter, then a following-sea shudder that eased by backing down to 15 knots.
body:
We were off the dock at St. Augustine at 5:45 this morning and headed for Charleston before the day was fully up.

By 6:08 we were out St. Augustine Inlet and turning north outside. The sun was coming up on another beautiful day, with a light one- to two-foot swell on the starboard quarter and the boat settling into an easy 17-knot run.

There are worse ways to start a day than that. So far it is another comfortable northbound leg with Charleston Safe Harbor ahead.

By 10:30 we were still running along nicely. The wind had clocked around and was knocking down the small seas we started with, but the following swell was putting a shudder through the boat that would both improve and get worse depending on whether the stabilizers were engaged or centered. It is one of those fiddly underway issues that does not feel completely natural, and my suspicion is that it may trace back to the all-glass enclosure added to the flybridge, or possibly the add-on hydraulic swim platform.

A little later the problem started to make more sense. We determined that the swim platform drags and the rudders do not engage adequately below about 15 knots. Backing down to 15 knots in the following seas took most of the shudder out of the boat, which at least gave us a workable answer. So the plan from there was simple enough: hold 15 knots and carry that into Charleston.

Even then the boat was still surfing now and then. The following swell would occasionally kick us up to 18 or 19 knots, but without the harmonics that had been rattling the flybridge, all while still turning 1750 rpm. Outside had gone hazy and there was that unmistakable smell of something burning ashore.

The radio also turned into a reminder of why the Coast Guard matters. We started hearing traffic about a person aboard a 26-foot boat roughly 50 miles east of Jacksonville who had suffered a heart attack. There was the usual confusion that comes when messages are being relayed through several different voices at once, with people trying to pin down exactly where the boat was and what the patient’s condition actually looked like. Even without hearing every side of the exchange, it was obvious the Coast Guard was handling it cleanly and professionally, and it sounded like they were also coordinating with the local sheriff while a few concerned boaters nearby helped relay what they could.

Before we ran out of range, we heard that a helicopter had been dispatched and that they were passing patient vitals while the crew worked to transfer him aboard. Listening to that unfold and hearing it handled so well does make you feel just a little safer being offshore. Semper Paratus.

The day ended in Charleston. We pulled into Charleston City Dock at 6:04, got fueled, and tied off for the night. After a long day offshore, that was enough.

title: Leaving Charleston Before Daylight
summary: Early grey departure from Charleston with weather on the mind and the boat settling into a 6 a.m. start.
body:
We were firing up the motors in Charleston at 5:36 this morning and getting ready to pull off the dock for Beaufort, North Carolina.

By 6:00 we were leaving the harbor in that early grey light, with one eye on the weather and the boat already settling into the day’s run.

Once properly underway, the next decision point came into focus. We were showing a 1:06 p.m. ETA to Frying Pan, and that was going to be the place where we checked the weather again and decided whether we were going to get forced inside from Cape Fear up to Beaufort.

The hope was that the forecast would slip a little and hold the stronger winds off until later in the afternoon. If it did, we could stay out on the ocean and make Beaufort at a reasonable hour instead of turning the day into an inside-route salvage job.

By early afternoon that question answered itself. We made the call to divert into Morningstar in Southport, North Carolina after a squall came through and brought 50-knot gusts, along with a free freshwater rinse-down whether we wanted one or not.

On the other side of it, the sea state had turned into the kind of mess that makes the decision for you: three feet of southbound chop stacked against three feet of northbound swell. Not horrible yet, but clearly deteriorating, and there was no point in pressing on toward Wrightsville Beach Inlet just to prove we could still be uncomfortable for longer.

In the end we landed safely at Morningstar Marina in Southport. We topped off the fuel, rinsed the boat down, and then used the extra time earned by stopping earlier than normal to catch up on engine-room housekeeping and get ready for tomorrow’s long push to Coinjock.

title: Leaving Morningstar for the ICW
summary: Sharp weather change on departure with 55-degree air and a 15-knot northeast wind as the trip shifted inland up the Cape Fear River toward the ICW.
body:
We were off the dock from Morningstar at 6:00 this morning and started up the Cape Fear River to begin the ICW portion of the trip.

By 6:30 we were heading up the river properly, with yesterday's offshore plan now behind us and the run shifting inland instead.

The main thing worth noting at departure was how dramatically the weather had changed. It was 55 degrees with a 15-knot northeast wind, which gave the morning a very different feel from the recent South Florida starts.

That changes the feel of the day. After the weather forced the stop in Southport, this morning starts as a more deliberate inside leg, pointed north again and back to the practical work of moving the boat up the line.

Some days do not go exactly according to plan, and this one turned into that kind of day. A mechanical issue slowed us down and forced us to stop in Beaufort, North Carolina instead of making the longer push we had in mind.

Once that happened, the focus shifted away from keeping up with the log and onto finding the quickest clean resolution. Between local recommendations and some internet digging, we were able to get the problem diagnosed and the failed parts removed before the end of the day, which was about as good an outcome as we could have hoped for once things started going sideways.

Service is lined up for first thing in the morning, so the delay looks manageable instead of open-ended. That is the part worth appreciating. Mechanical problems are part of being at sea, and in a different place this could easily have turned into a much longer and more frustrating layover.

Instead, Beaufort turned out to be a pretty good place to get stuck for a day. The interruption was unexpected, but it looks like we should be able to get moving again quickly, and there are worse places to spend an extra day while the boat gets put back in order.

That extra day alongside gives us room to handle repairs properly, catch up on systems maintenance, and do some cleaning so the rest of the run goes more smoothly once we are moving again.
